tagline.text: A mangrove eco-park with a bamboo walkway, grown from the mudflats of Kalibo into 220 hectares of forest

location.label: Location
location.text: Barangay New Buswang, Kalibo, Aklan, about 4 km from downtown Kalibo

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱200~800 (per person, entrance fee, tricycle and meals, from downtown Kalibo)

children.text: Bakhawan Eco-Park is a 220-hectare forest grown from mangroves planted on the Kalibo mudflats beginning in 1990. You can walk a bamboo walkway of about 1.3 km through the trees, paddle a kayak, plant a seedling and even try tamilok, all in half a day.

Bakhawan Eco-Park is a mangrove forest in Barangay New Buswang in Kalibo, the capital of Aklan. "Bakhawan" is the local word for mangrove. It sits on the coast roughly 4 km from Kalibo's busy streets, and Wikipedia gives its area as 220 hectares (about 540 acres). The forest is man-made. The site was once a muddy shoreline with nothing to shield it from the sea, and residents and civic groups began planting trees there to protect the community from floods and storm surges.

It all began in 1989, when the Kalibo Save the Mangroves Association (KASAMA) proposed turning the Kalibo mudflats into a mangrove plantation. The following year, 1990, the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) granted a loan to the municipality of Kalibo, and 250,000 trees were planted on 50 hectares of reclaimed coastline. Over more than three decades, natural regeneration and replanting have grown the forest to about five times its original size. Wikipedia calls the project the Philippines' most successful mangrove reforestation effort, and the UN Food and Agriculture Organization has cited it as an exemplary case in Asia and the Pacific. KASAMA still runs the park today and is now a registered multipurpose cooperative.

In November 2013, Typhoon Haiyan (Yolanda) swept across the central Philippines and badly damaged mangroves as well. On January 22, 2014, the Aklan provincial government planted 8,000 new mangrove seedlings on 2 hectares to prepare for climate change and replace the lost trees. The forest is therefore not a finished attraction but a protected forest that is still being tended and expanded, which is why letting visitors plant trees themselves is a key part of the program.

For travelers this is an easy half-day trip from downtown Kalibo. Past the information desk and souvenir shop at the entrance, a bamboo walkway leads deep into the forest and ends at a shore that opens toward the Sibuyan Sea. It suits you if you have a free half day in Kalibo on the way to Boracay, or if you want a quiet place away from the midday heat and crowds during the Ati-Atihan festival. Even slow walkers can manage it, but there is little shade, so bring a hat and water.
A bamboo walkway of about
1.3 km
through the forest is the heart of the park. It sits a few meters above the ground and may seem to creak at first, but it is sturdy. Walking slowly takes more than
30 minutes
, and some blogs give the length as 1.1 km, so think of it as "a little over 1 km."

blocks.title: A shoreline view at the end of the forest

children.text: The walkway ends at a shore where mangrove seedlings have been planted, and the view opens toward the Sibuyan Sea. There are rest huts along the way, and the floor and bamboo fences of the last shelter are covered in graffiti left by visitors.

At the shore at the end of the walkway, visitors can plant mangrove seedlings themselves. It is a hands-on way to understand why this forest was created, and you can ask the staff at the entrance how to join and what it costs.
You can ride a kayak or a bamboo raft along the channels between the mangroves. At low tide the trips may not be possible, so check the tide on site.
Around the

mark on the walkway, park keepers split rotting mangrove logs to take out tamilok. Tamilok is not a worm but a shell-less mollusk. The heads and tails are removed, and the meat is soaked in vinegar for about
5 minutes
and served kilawin style with sinamak, the spiced vinegar of Panay. The texture is said to be like an oyster, and you need to request it in advance.

The forest shelters many birds and marine animals. One visitor account mentions a blue kingfisher that was not bothered by people. You can also see mud crabs and fish that locals catch, which makes the park a fit for anyone who enjoys birdwatching.

Wikipedia lists a Center for International Mangrove Studies, a watchtower, a charcoal briquetting area and a massage area among the park's facilities. The charcoal area began as a livelihood project for residents, and whether each facility is operating can differ from visit to visit.
You can rent a cottage facing the sea to rest. A 2022 price list shows a cottage rental of
. It is a nice place for a picnic lunch, but it costs extra, so confirm at the entrance.
Take a tricycle from downtown Kalibo to Bakhawan Eco-Park in New Buswang. It takes about
15 minutes
from town, and it helps to arrange your ride back in advance.
Pay the entrance fee at the entrance and look around the information desk and souvenir shop. If you want a guide, decide now.
Walk the bamboo walkway slowly. Watch for birds and mudflat life, and take photos.
Near the
mark, ask to try tamilok (request in advance). Plant a seedling at the shore.
Rest at a shelter or cottage, and take a kayak out if time allows.
Return to downtown Kalibo for lunch.
There is little shade at midday, so choose early morning or late afternoon if you can. Activities on the water depend on the tide.
See the walkway and the shore at Bakhawan Eco-Park.
Return to downtown Kalibo and have lunch at a restaurant.
Walk through the town center sights, including St. John the Baptist Cathedral, Pastrana Park and the museum.
Pick up snacks at a cafe or market, then head to your hotel or the airport.
There are direct flights from Manila's Ninoy Aquino International Airport to Kalibo International Airport (KLO), taking about
1 hour
. Check airlines and schedules when you book.
From KLO you can reach downtown Kalibo by tricycle, taxi or shared ride. Check fares locally.
From the Caticlan jetty for Boracay, you can reach Kalibo by van or bus. Travel time varies with traffic, so confirm with the driver or the information desk before boarding.
Going from Kalibo to Caticlan is possible as a half-day trip after downtown, but check the last departure in advance.
In downtown Kalibo, take a tricycle and say "Bakhawan Eco-Park, New Buswang." Many blogs say it takes about
10~15 minutes
Tricycle fares change with the season and with bargaining. One 2014 blog reports paying
including a wait for the return trip. It may have gone up since, so agree on the price before you ride.

The park's phone is (036) 262 8862, its email is kasama.inc17@gmail.com and its Facebook page is "Bakhawan Nature Study and Eco-park." Hours and fees can change, so it is safest to inquire before you go.

Walking the mangrove forest is best in the dry season, from November to May, because rain makes the walkway slippery and clouds the view over the shore. Even in the dry season the midday sun is strong, so go in the early morning or late afternoon.

The Ati-Atihan festival is held in Kalibo every January and is when the town is at its busiest. Lodging and transport get crowded, so plan the eco-park for a quieter day around the festival or for early morning. Festival dates change each year, so check the latest announcements.

There is no lodging in the park, and travelers usually stay in downtown Kalibo or on Boracay. Downtown Kalibo has small hotels and guesthouses near the airport, handy for early flights or late arrivals. Check the latest reviews and rates on a booking site. Many itineraries see the park first and then rest in town, or go straight on toward Caticlan.

The park has a souvenir shop that sells snacks and bottled water, and you can try tamilok if you ask ahead. The easiest way to eat is to return to downtown Kalibo, which also has more choices. The menu and hours of any restaurant inside the park could not be confirmed, so it is fine to bring a packed lunch and water. Tamilok is eaten raw after soaking in vinegar, so there is no need to force it if you are squeamish.
When you take a tricycle, ask the driver to wait for the ride back, or ask first whether you can catch another in front of the park.
Walking slowly takes more than
30 minutes
. If you want to take photos at an easy pace, allow an hour or more.
For birdwatching, early morning is best, and binoculars help.
Tamilok and tree planting must be requested in advance, so tell the staff at the entrance early.
There is little shade at midday, so bring a hat, sunscreen and water, and mosquito repellent is also useful.
Fees and hours differ from blog to blog, so confirm them on site. Many accounts say the park opens between 7 and 8 AM and closes between 5 and 6 PM.
Wear sandals or sneakers that do not slip, and watch that your feet do not catch in the gaps of the bamboo floor.
Many places want cash, so bring plenty of small bills.
Entrance fees and opening hours differ by year and by source. The 2025 blog and the 2022 price list do not match, so check directly with the park before your visit.
The bamboo walkway is slippery in the rain and some sections may be worn, so hold the handrail as you walk.
At low tide the mudflats are exposed and kayaks or rafts may not run.
Tamilok is raw food, so skip it if hygiene worries you.
This is a protected forest, so do not break branches or disturb birds and mudflat animals, and take your trash with you.
The walkway can get dark after sunset, so return early in the afternoon.
About
10~15 minutes
from the eco-park, the Aklan capital
Kalibo
has a cathedral, a market and a museum within walking distance.
The
Ati-Atihan Festival
, held in Kalibo every January, is one of the Philippines' best-known festivals in honor of the Santo Niño.
Boracay
, reached from Kalibo Airport by road and boat, is the country's most famous beach destination.
The cathedral, park and museum in central Kalibo go well with the eco-park as a half-day downtown route.
